# Causal setup

## Two questions that are not alternatives

Write \(X\) for the prompt ending immediately before the article,
\(B\in\{\texttt{a},\texttt{an}\}\) for the article token, and \(Y\) for
the next-token distribution over the first content **noun token**.
Outcomes are lexical / noun-token identity, not semantic-concept rewrite
(`lawyer`\(\leftrightarrow\)`attorney` may keep occupation meaning while
changing the token). An internal intervention \(I\) is applied at the last
prompt position \(P\) and **kept on** during noun prediction.

Two questions are independent (@fig-schematic, left). The first is about
**content**: does the intervened state at \(P\) represent phonological
article class, a specific noun token, or a coarser concept? The second is
about **transmission**: after \(I\) is applied, does a later noun change
travel through the identity of the generated article, or remain after that
article is held fixed? Generated-token mediation answers the second
question. It does not rule out a latent plan at \(P\). A fused
article--noun package and a modular plan can both produce large
free-generation noun changes that are still carried by the written
article.

Left: \(I_t\) can affect \(Y_{t+2}\) through the visible article \(B_{t+1}\) or through private contextual state \(H_P\); \(\operatorname{do}(B)\) clamps public token identity, while a residual patch at \(P\) intervenes on the private path. Right: intervention off/on crossed with free generation and inserted \(\texttt{a}\) or \(\texttt{an}\).](manuscript/figures/fig_hypotheses_protocol.png){#fig-schematic width=96%}

## Six-cell design and vector identity

For every prompt we run six forwards:

$$
I\in\{\text{off},\text{on}\}
\times
B\in\{\text{free},\operatorname{do}(\texttt{a}),
\operatorname{do}(\texttt{an})\}.
$$

Free cells let the model write the article. Inserted-article cells paste
`a` or `an` and then predict the noun. This is a **natural-and-controlled**
design, not an assigned \(2\times 3\) factorial: `free` is a policy, not a
treatment level of \(B\). Write \(B_0\) and \(B_1\) for the greedy articles
under \(I=\text{off}\) and \(I=\text{on}\), and write \(Y(i,b)\) for the
noun distribution. Define the free-generation **total** change, the
**token-substitution** (treated-token replay) change, and the
**matched-prefix leftover** under the treated article:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_T &= Y(1,B_1)-Y(0,B_0),\\
E_M &= Y(0,B_1)-Y(0,B_0),\\
E_R &= Y(1,B_1)-Y(0,B_1).
\end{aligned}
$$

These are probability vectors, so
\(E_T=E_M+E_R\) holds exactly for every prompt whose free articles are
`a` or `an`. Total variation of those vectors is **not** additive and is
not a percent mediated. We therefore report TV of each piece, cosine of
\(E_M\) and of \(E_R\) with \(E_T\), and the reconstruction
\(\|E_T-(E_M+E_R)\|_1\) as an implementation check. We also report
matched-prefix leftovers under **both** inserted articles, including the
article the intervention does not select. Distances use full-vocabulary
TV; target-minus-source logits on seven prompts with listed
cross-class twins are a second readout. Multi-token nouns are
teacher-forced token by token.

We never write "direct effect" for a leftover without naming the
fixed article. The leftover \(E_R\) is a controlled contrast under
treated-article insertion, not Pearl's natural direct effect.

## Non-identifiability of leftover control from free generation

**Identification observation.** A large free-generation change in \(Y\) does not identify
leftover internal control of the noun. If \(I\) changes only \(B\) and
\(Y\) depends on \(B\), then \(E_T\) can be large while \(E_R=0\). If \(I\)
also changes noun computation after \(B\) is fixed, \(E_R\) is nonzero.
Observing \(E_T\) alone cannot distinguish those cases, nor distinguish a
fused package from a modular plan. The six cells separate token
substitution from matched-prefix leftover; they still do not identify
semantic content at \(P\).

## Intervention, outcomes, and uncertainty

The sparse intervention is multiplicative on prompt-specific activations
at \(P\):

$$
z_f \leftarrow \texttt{amplify\_factor}\times z_f(X,P)
$$

for each selected feature \(f\). The default gain is \(5\times\); dose
runs use \(1.5\times\) and \(3\times\). Large multiplicative gains can be
off-manifold; dose and a matched random control bound that concern.
Feature sets were **fixed before the six-cell runs** from attribution
graphs on eight selection occupations disjoint from the 20 held-out
prompts. Nouns observed after free generation are post hoc and used only
descriptively. Primary noun sampling is **greedy decoding**. Confidence
intervals are prompt-level nonparametric bootstrap intervals with 10,000
resamples.

## Reachability and positive control

Inserting an article does not erase earlier hidden states: later layers
can attend to position \(P\). We verify reachability by measuring sparse
CLT activation changes at the inserted-article position after applying S1
at \(P\). Separately, we patch the complete decoder-layer output residual
at the inserted-article position. Layer selection uses four development
pairs; the selected layer is evaluated on four held-out same-article-class
pairs against ten matched-norm random directions. This is a
stack-sensitivity reference, not an oracle and not evidence that S1
encodes the same lexical information.

## Separately intervenable public and private routes

Fixing the article token does not fix contextual hidden state. A surviving
effect may travel from the intervened pre-article position \(P\) even when
the visible article is identical. Write \(B\) for the **public token
identity** and \(H\) for **private contextual state** propagated from
\(P\). These are experimentally separable causes in this task, not
independent registers carrying the same lexical plan, and not a direct
edit of the hidden state underneath the written article [@shih2026registers].

We construct a target-state reference using source/target lexical cues whose
nouns share native article `a`. At selected layer \(\ell\), \(H=0\) leaves
the source residual at \(P\) unchanged and \(H=1\) replaces it with the
target-cued residual,

$$
h_P^{(\ell)} \leftarrow h_P^{(\ell)}(X_{\mathrm{target}}).
$$

Matched-norm random controls replace the same residual by
\(h_P^{(\ell)}(X_{\mathrm{source}})+\| \delta \| \, r/\|r\|\), where
\(\delta=h_P^{(\ell)}(X_{\mathrm{target}})-h_P^{(\ell)}(X_{\mathrm{source}})\)
and \(r\) is a standard Gaussian vector. We cross this with inserted
\(B\in\{\texttt{a},\texttt{an}\}\). Define

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_b &= Y(H=1,b)-Y(H=0,b),\\
P_h &= Y(h,\texttt{an})-Y(h,\texttt{a}),\\
\Gamma &= L_{\texttt{an}}-L_{\texttt{a}}=P_1-P_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Primary private-route inference uses the paired differences
\(D_i=L_{\texttt{a},i}^{\mathrm{target}}-\overline{L_{\texttt{a},i}^{\mathrm{random}}}\)
and
\(\Gamma_i^{\mathrm{target}}-\overline{\Gamma_i^{\mathrm{random}}}\).
The patch is a capacity/reference intervention, not evidence that S1
naturally carries the same lexical state.
